discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.
How do you decide what to eat?

Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about
why or why not.

Imagine you decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in
your life for you to do that?

What might make plant-based foods more appealing to you or other men
you know?

Okay everyone, that’s our time. Thanks so much for participating
today. Before we finish, is there anything else you would like to add
about food choices, gender, masculinity, or plant-based eating?

transcript.content: Hi everyone, thanks for joining today. We're going to spend around 45 minutes talking about food choices — what you eat, why you eat it, and some thoughts on plant-based food in particular. The session is being recorded for research purposes, but there are no right or wrong answers here — we're genuinely just interested in your experiences and views. You don't need to take turns formally; if something comes to mind, feel free to jump in. Just try to keep space for each other. To get us started, let's go around and do quick introductions — just your name and whereabouts in the UK you're coming from today.
Yeah hi, I'm Amir, I'm from Birmingham — well, born and raised here basically. Yeah that's me.
Hi, I'm David, based in Glasgow — well, just outside it really. Looking forward to the chat.
Hi yeah, I'm Isaiah, from Leeds — well, born in Sheffield but been in Leeds a few years now. Good to meet you all.
Yeah, hi everyone — I'm Ibrahim, from Newcastle. Born and raised there, still there now. Good to meet you all.
Yeah, good to meet you all. David, you're practically a neighbour then — well, relatively speaking. Rural Scotland's a bit of a different world from Glasgow but still.

Great, good to have everyone here — Birmingham, Glasgow, Leeds, Newcastle, and rural Scotland. Quite the spread. Okay, let's get into it. I want to start with something fairly everyday: thinking about a typical week, how do you actually decide what to eat? Not in an ideal-world sense — just what actually drives it day to day.

For me it's pretty much just practicality, yeah. Like, I don't have a big supermarket nearby so it's whatever's available locally, what I've got in. We've got a good butcher not far away so I tend to use that. It's not really a conscious decision to eat meat or whatever, it's just... that's what's there and it's what works. I'm not sitting there planning meals out for the week or anything like that.

Yeah that resonates — I'm similar in that it's mostly convenience and habit driving it. Being just outside Glasgow I've got access to supermarkets but I still tend to just grab what I know, what's quick. It's not like I'm making ethical decisions every meal.

Yeah exactly, convenience is massive. Like Birmingham's got everything — you've got your Lidls, your Aldis, halal butchers everywhere, proper curry houses, all sorts — but even with all that I still just end up doing the same rotation basically. Chicken most days, bit of lamb here and there, whatever's easy to chuck together after uni or whatever. It's not like I'm thinking about it that much.

Yeah same here really. Like Newcastle's got a decent bit of variety but I still end up doing the same rotation. Mam's cooking's a big influence — grew up eating certain things so that's just what feels normal to make myself now. Lamb, chicken, bit of fish sometimes. It's not really a conscious choice, it's just... that's what food is to me, if that makes sense.

So across the group there's a lot of common ground here — convenience, habit, eating what you grew up with. I want to push on that a bit, because I'm curious whether it's ever more deliberate than that. Has there been a time — a specific moment, a shop, a meal — where you actually made a real choice rather than just defaulting? Where something pushed you to eat differently from what you'd normally do, and you went with it or didn't? I'm interested in whether anyone has a different experience from what's been said — or a moment where the habit broke.

Yeah I've got something on this actually. When I first moved to Leeds I was living with a mate who was vegetarian, and just for ease of it, like, we were sharing cooking and stuff, I ended up eating basically what he ate for a few months. Barely touched meat.

And it was fine, like I wasn't suffering or anything. But then one day I just really fancied a proper steak and I thought — why am I not eating this? This isn't a choice I actually made, I just drifted into it.

So I went back to eating meat, but it was kind of the first time I'd actually consciously picked it rather than just doing it by habit. Which was a weird feeling. Like the habit had flipped without me deciding to flip it, and then I had to actually decide to flip it back.

I don't know what that says about anything really, but it made me realise how much of what you eat is just circumstance rather than proper choice. Either way, vegetarian or not.

Isaiah, that's interesting — the habit flipping without you deciding it, and then having to actively choose to flip it back. Does that land differently for anyone else? I'm curious whether others have had moments where the direction was similar — or the other way around.

Yeah that's interesting Isaiah. I had something similar but kind of the reverse — went travelling for a bit, Southeast Asia, and ended up eating way more meat than I normally would just because of what was on offer everywhere, street food and that. And when I came back I realised I'd just drifted into eating differently without deciding to.

Didn't really prompt any big reflection about it though, I just sort of... went back to normal gradually. But yeah, the point about circumstance just shaping it without you noticing — that rings true.

Yeah that's actually really relatable. The halal thing is a big factor for me — like at home or when I'm buying from the butcher I know it's halal so it's straightforward. But if I'm round a mate's or somewhere I'm not sure, I'll just not bother with the meat rather than make a fuss about it. Not a principled decision, just easier to avoid the hassle.

So yeah it is circumstance a lot of the time. But I don't think I'd say I drifted away from meat and then had to choose to go back like Isaiah did — it's more like meat's still the default, I just temporarily can't access the right version of it if that makes sense.

Yeah that's exactly my situation too, Amir. Like I'll just go for the veggie option if I'm not sure about the meat somewhere, but I'm not thinking "oh maybe I should eat less meat" — I'm just waiting until I can get the right thing. The default hasn't shifted at all, you're just kind of paused temporarily.

Yeah the default thing rings true for me too. But I think for me it's even more like... the environment's never really tested it? Like Isaiah, you had the flatmate situation, David you were travelling — something external actually pushed against your normal. For me living out here, nothing's really changed. The butcher's always been there, my family always ate this way, I've never really been in a situation where I had to think about it differently.

So I do wonder if my "default" is just more... set, I suppose? Not because I've thought about it and decided, just because nothing's ever come along to nudge it.

Will, that's a useful way to put it — the default that's never really been tested because the circumstances haven't changed. That feels like a different thing from what Isaiah and David described, where something external actually pushed against the habit, even if only temporarily. So we've got a few different pictures here — defaults that drift without you noticing, defaults that pause but don't shift, and defaults that have never really been challenged at all. I want to move on to something related, because I think what's underneath a lot of what you've said is worth exploring more directly. Thinking about your food choices — do you think being a man has anything to do with what you eat, or how you think about food? Why or why not?

Yeah I think there is something to it — not in a way I've ever really articulated before, but like... red meat especially, burgers, a big steak, there's definitely a vibe around that being a "man's food" that I've absorbed somewhere. Adverts, banter with mates, that kind of thing.

But I wouldn't say it actually drives my choices consciously. Like I don't eat a steak and think "yeah this is masculine." It's more just... background noise? Something that's there but I couldn't tell you where it came from or how much it actually affects anything.
Isaiah, I haven't heard from you yet on this one — does what David's describing ring true from your experience, or does it sit differently for you?

Yeah David's background noise thing is exactly it for me. I couldn't have put it better.

And actually going back to my steak moment — I've been thinking about it while you were all talking — I reckon part of what pulled me back wasn't just fancying it taste-wise. There was something about it feeling... normal again? Like properly normal, in a way that went a bit beyond just the food itself.

I can't tell you it was definitely a masculinity thing because I wasn't sitting there thinking that. But there was something about the vegetarian period that felt a bit like I was just going along with someone else's thing, and the steak felt like me reasserting something. What exactly, I'm not totally sure.

So yeah, background noise feels right. It's there, I just can't fully trace where it comes from or how much it's actually doing.
Isaiah, you said the steak felt like reasserting something — but you said you're not totally sure what. Can you say a bit more about what you mean by that?

Yeah... I think if I'm honest it was about identity more than anything. Like during that three months I did feel slightly like I'd become a different version of myself, but without having actually decided to. And going back to meat felt like — I don't know, like getting back to a version of me I recognised.

Whether that's tied up with being a man specifically or just being me as a person, I genuinely can't separate those two things out. Like I can't tell you which one it was because they're kind of the same thing to me. My sense of who I am and my sense of being a bloke — they're not separate boxes.

So I don't know if that answers it or just makes it more complicated. It wasn't a conscious masculinity thing. But it was definitely an identity thing, and identity's probably got masculinity in it somewhere whether I'm aware of it or not.

Isaiah, thanks — that idea of them not being separate boxes is worth sitting with. So we've heard from David and Isaiah on this. What about the rest of you — does gender come into it at all for how you think about what you eat, or is that not really how it feels from where you're sitting?

Yeah I mean gender's not really how I'd frame it for me personally. Like I don't think about eating meat as a male thing particularly.

But what Isaiah said about identity — that does land. For me it's more the halal side of it. Like that's so wrapped up in who I am that I don't even clock it most of the time, it's just... part of how I eat, part of how I exist. And if I'm somewhere where that's not possible it does feel slightly off, not in a massive way but just a bit like something's not quite right.

So yeah, identity's definitely in there for me. Just not through the gender angle so much.

Yeah that's interesting Amir, because what you're describing — not even clocking it most of the time — is kind of the opposite of how I experienced it. Like I only noticed the identity stuff when it was disrupted. When it was just normal I wasn't thinking about it at all, same as you. It only became visible when it was gone.

Which maybe says something about how deep that stuff runs. You don't see it until something removes it.

Yeah exactly that. Like I genuinely don't think about halal on a normal day — it's just the way things are. It's only when I'm somewhere unfamiliar or I can't be sure about it that I suddenly become aware of it as a thing. Like it surfaces only when there's friction.

So there's something the group seems to be landing on here — this idea that the identity stuff in food is basically invisible until something gets in the way. Isaiah noticed it when the habit was disrupted by living with his mate. Amir and David have both described a similar thing — it's just there, below the surface, and you only clock it when something creates friction. I want to test that a bit, because I'm wondering if it's the full picture. Is there anyone who can think of a moment where it wasn't like that — where being a man, or the expectations around it, was actually present and conscious at the time, not just something you noticed afterwards? A situation where you were making a food choice and the gender thing was actively in the room, not just background noise you recognised later?

Yeah actually — uni was like that for me. Not a gender thing exactly, but the halal thing in social situations. Like someone would just hand you a burger at a party or whatever and you'd have to say no, and there'd be this moment where you could see them thinking you were being awkward about it. And I was definitely aware in that moment of how I was coming across — like am I being difficult, am I making this weird. It wasn't something I figured out afterwards, it was right there at the time.

So I get what you're asking about it being conscious and present rather than just background. It was that for me, just through the halal angle rather than specifically a masculinity thing.
Thanks Ibrahim. Will — I haven't heard from you yet on this one, and I'm curious whether any of what's been said connects to your experience at all.

Yeah, I can think of moments like that. Not really gender specifically but — at school, like, if you weren't eating enough at lunch or you were being fussy about something, you'd get ribbed for it. And you were definitely aware of it at the time, it wasn't something you looked back on later and thought oh that was about fitting in. It was right there in the moment.

So yeah, that conscious thing the moderator's describing — I get that. It just wasn't specifically about being male for me, it was more just... not wanting to stand out or seem like you were being difficult about food. Which I suppose is what Ibrahim's describing too, just through a different route.

So I want to try to pull together what's come out across the group on this, because I think there's something worth naming. Every one of you has described a moment where food and identity were genuinely connected — Isaiah's steak, Amir and Ibrahim navigating halal in unfamiliar situations, Will getting ribbed at school for being fussy. And in every single case, when you've gone to put a name on what the identity thing actually was, gender hasn't been the word anyone's reached for. It's been religion, it's been habit, it's been just not wanting to stand out. I'm not saying that's wrong — it might be exactly right. But I want to test it directly, because the question I started with was specifically about being male. So I'll ask it plainly: is there a moment any of you can think of where being a man — not just wanting to fit in, not the halal situation, but specifically the male bit — actually shaped what you ate or didn't eat? Or is the honest answer that it doesn't really show up that way for you?

I mean, I already said there's background noise around red meat and masculinity. But trying to think of an actual moment where the male bit was specifically the thing... it's hard to pin down.

The closest I can get is maybe like — there are certain situations where I'd feel a bit self-conscious ordering something that might come across as fussy or delicate. Like a really elaborate salad or something. Not because I'm consciously thinking "that's not manly," more just... something about how it'd land with certain people. Certain mates, say.

But even saying that out loud it feels a bit thin, you know? I can't point to a specific moment and say yeah, that was genuinely about being male. It might just be about not wanting to seem precious about food generally, which is what Will was describing too.

So I think the honest answer is — maybe it's there, but I can't clearly separate it out from just general social stuff about fitting in.

David, you said the salad thing feels thin — but I want to stay with it for a second before we move on. You mentioned 'certain mates' specifically. When you imagine ordering something like that in front of them, what do you think it would actually signal to them about you?

Yeah, okay. I think it would signal something like... being precious about food. High-maintenance maybe. Like someone who overthinks what they eat.

And actually thinking about it more — that does feel like it's got a male dimension to it specifically, not just general fitting in. There's something about just getting on with it, not making food into a big deal, that feels like part of how that particular group operates. Like as lads. You just eat, you don't fuss about it.

So maybe it's less thin than I made it sound. It's not that eating a salad would make them think I was less of a man in some obvious way — it's more subtle than that. It's about not being the kind of person who makes a thing out of what they eat. And I think that expectation does run along male lines in that specific group, yeah.

David, so the thing it would signal is being precious — high-maintenance — and you're saying that expectation runs specifically along male lines in that group.
